evidence: Varr. RR 3.16.6: itaque iīs ūnctus quī accessit, pungunt
Petr. 56: Ideō autem pungunt, quia ubīcunque dulce est, ibi et acidum inveniēs.
terms.comment: Of bees in Varro and in Trimalchio’s talk. Of a nettle Latin says it burns, ūrit (see “nettle”).

terms.gloss: it bites (a dog, a flea, a snake)
evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 57: aliī canēs, quī et lātrāre et mordēre possunt
Curt. 7.4: canem timidum vehementius lātrāre quam mordēre

phrases.english: Watch out for the bee: it stings!

phrases.latin: Mordetne hic canis? — Nōn mordet; lēniter eum mulcē.
phrases.english: Does this dog bite? — No, it doesn’t; stroke it gently.

phrases.latin: mīlia crābrōnum coeunt, et vertice nūdō spīcula dēfīgunt ōraque sīma notant
phrases.english: hornets swarm in thousands, drive their stings into his bald head, and mark his snub-nosed face (Silenus raiding a hive)

phrases.latin: Apēs enim ego dīvīnās bēstiās putō … Ideō autem pungunt, quia ubīcunque dulce est, ibi et acidum inveniēs.
phrases.english: I think bees are heavenly creatures … And the reason they sting is that wherever there’s something sweet you’ll find something sour too.
It doesn’t bite; it won’t hurt you.

phrases.latin: Nē timē: apis nōn pungit, nisi eam laeseris.
phrases.english: Don’t be afraid: the bee won’t sting unless you hurt it.

sources: Lewis & Short: pungo · Lewis & Short: mordeo
